newsitem.title: FRANCE: French rail strike ends, Air France protest starts.
newsitem.headline: French rail strike ends, Air France protest starts.

text.p: Passenger rail services were near normal in France on Monday after a five-day train conductors' strike, but travellers braced for a four-day strike by Air France pilots set to begin on Tuesday.
The French rail authority SNCF said most conductors had returned to work on Monday after disrupting rail traffic over a long holiday weekend.
"On Tuesday, traffic will be near normal across the country, apart from a few lines where service will be slightly reduced," the SNCF said in a statement.
About one in three trains had been cancelled on most main lines between Wednesday and Sunday in the dispute over staffing levels and bonuses.
The stoppage had spared high-speed Eurostar trains to London through the Channel Tunnel as well as high-speed trains between Paris and Brussels.
Air France has urged pilots and engineers to ignore union calls for this week's four-day strike, saying it would wipe out the entire year's profit at the state-owned airline.
Managers have been instructed to maintain regular flight schedules from Tuesday through Friday despite the strike call by six unions.

The strike is to protest against planned wage cuts and changes in working conditions under a merger between long-distance carrier Air France and its European arm, Air France Europe. The merger is intended to make the carriers more competitive as European routes open up to cross-border competition.

Air France accuses the unions of stoking the conflict by calling a strike while negotiations are under way on the points of disagreement and believes many of the pilots and flight engineers oppose the strike and will not participate.
The SNPL pilots union said an independent study shows the wages proposed for new pilots at the state-owned group are lower than those paid by Lufthansa, British Airways and KLM.

Air France wants to hire 450 pilots in the next year and a half and would pay them gross starting salaries of 220,000 francs ($38,260) a year, a third less than what was paid to the pilots now on staff.
